name: Mock Test 04
description: A full-length, high-difficulty CELPIP-General style exam: 6 Listening, 4 Reading, 2 Writing, and 8 Speaking sections in the official order, with multi-step reasoning, close distractors, and official speaking timings.

sections.title: Part 1 · Listening to Problem Solving
sections.instructions: Listen to the conversation and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
COORDINATOR: Harbourfront Conference Centre, Marcus speaking.
CALLER: Hello Marcus, it's Lena Petrov from the Pacific Nurses Association. I got an email saying the Ballroom for our March fourteenth workshop has been double-booked. We're expecting ninety people.
COORDINATOR: I'm very sorry about that, Ms. Petrov. A corporate booking was entered manually, and our system didn't flag the overlap. I can offer three alternatives. Room B is free at the same time, nine to four, but it seats only sixty. Room C seats one hundred, but it isn't available until one o'clock, so you'd run from one to eight in the evening. Or we could move the whole event to Saturday the sixteenth in the Ballroom, and I'd take fifteen percent off the rental.
CALLER: Sixty won't work; we'd have to turn away thirty people. And Saturday is a problem because many of our members work weekend shifts. What would Room C cost?
COORDINATOR: Normally it's three hundred fifty dollars more than the Ballroom, but given the circumstances, I can waive that difference.
CALLER: That helps. But an afternoon start changes our lunch plans. We had catering booked for noon.
COORDINATOR: Our kitchen can convert that into a dinner buffet at six at the same per-person price. Since the event is more than a week away, there's no penalty for changing the menu.
CALLER: Actually, an afternoon start might suit our keynote speaker. She flies in from Vancouver at ten that morning. But she'll need a projector and a microphone.
COORDINATOR: The projector is included. The wireless microphone system is normally seventy-five dollars, and I'll include that at no charge. One thing, though: I need your confirmation by five o'clock today, because another client has shown interest in Room C.
CALLER: I have to check with our board chair first. Could you hold it until tomorrow at noon?
COORDINATOR: The latest I can hold it is ten tomorrow morning. After that I'm required to release it.
CALLER: All right. I'll call you before then.

questions.question: What caused the double booking?
options: Two clients paid deposits on the same day
The Pacific Nurses Association confirmed its booking late
The Ballroom was undergoing repairs
Another booking was entered manually without the system flagging the overlap
questions.explanation: Marcus says a corporate booking was entered manually and the overlap wasn't flagged.

MIA: That's the thing. I was in Lisbon for the whole second month, so paying half feels unfair. But I don't think it should all fall on you either, since the fridge and the internet router kept running the entire time.

sections.passage: ANNOUNCER: Residents of Millbrook will face a longer wait for the reopening of the Harper Street Bridge. City engineers announced today that the bridge, which closed on June third for a full deck replacement, will now reopen on October thirtieth instead of September fifteenth. The city cited a delay in the delivery of structural steel and unexpectedly severe corrosion found in the support beams. The estimated cost has risen from twelve million to fourteen and a half million dollars. In the meantime, drivers are directed along a seven-kilometre detour via Route Nine, and bus route twenty-two has been rerouted, adding roughly fifteen minutes to each trip. Business owners near the bridge say foot traffic is down by about a quarter, and some are asking the city for temporary property tax relief. A city spokesperson said council will consider the request at its next session but noted that no decision has been made. Pedestrian and cycling access is scheduled to be restored on August twentieth.

sections.title: Part 6 · Listening for Viewpoints
sections.instructions: Listen to the two speakers and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
SPEAKER A: I think cities should allow short-term rentals with light regulation. For many homeowners, renting out a spare room is what keeps them able to pay the mortgage. And visitors spend money in neighbourhoods that hotels never reach; they shop at corner cafés, not just downtown.
SPEAKER B: But the evidence from cities that allowed it is troubling. When landlords realize they can earn more from weekend visitors than from a long-term tenant, they convert apartments into de facto hotels, and rents rise. In one study, the neighbourhoods with the most listings saw rents climb nearly twice as fast as the city average.
SPEAKER A: That's a fair concern, but it points to regulation, not prohibition. Cities can cap the number of nights an entire unit may be rented, say ninety a year, while still letting people rent a room in the home where they live.
SPEAKER B: Caps sound good on paper, but enforcement is notoriously difficult. Cities need staff to track listings, and the platforms haven't always cooperated. I'd also add that noise and constant turnover erode the sense of community in apartment buildings.
SPEAKER A: Enforcement is a challenge, but it isn't unique to this issue. And I'd argue that banning outright pushes the activity underground, where there is no safety oversight at all.

questions.label: Question 1
questions.question: What is Speaker A's overall position?
options: They should be unregulated
They should be banned in all residential areas
They should be limited to hotels
Short-term rentals should be allowed with light regulation
questions.explanation: Speaker A supports allowing rentals with light regulation.

sections.passage:
From: Priya Nair <priya.nair@mailbox.ca>
To: Colin Beck <colin@beckbuilders.ca>
Subject: Concerns about revised kitchen costs

Dear Colin,

I have reviewed the revised estimate you sent on Monday, and I have several concerns. Our original quote was $18,500, and I paid the 30 percent deposit on April 1. The new estimate adds $1,200 to replace wiring behind the north wall, plus $640 for the under-cabinet lighting, and pushes completion from May 3 to May 17.

I understand surprises happen in older houses, but you inspected the kitchen twice before giving me the quote, and wiring was never mentioned. I feel the wiring cost should not fall entirely on me. I would also like to know whether the delay will affect the warranty.

I look forward to your reply.

Priya Nair

------------------------------

From: Colin Beck <colin@beckbuilders.ca>
To: Priya Nair
Subject: Re: Concerns about revised kitchen costs

Dear Priya,

Thank you for raising this directly. I want to be transparent about how the numbers came about.

The wiring was concealed behind the drywall, so it could not have been seen during either inspection. Section 4 of our contract excludes concealed conditions from the fixed price, which is why it appears as an additional cost. That said, I recognize the wiring is not something you could have anticipated, so as a gesture of goodwill I will cover half of it. Your share would be $600 instead of $1,200.

The lighting is different. It was an optional upgrade that you requested on April 10, so I am unable to reduce that cost. With these adjustments, your revised total would be $19,740.

The completion date of May 17 is firm, provided the electrician's inspection passes on schedule. The two-year warranty on labour is unaffected by the delay. The remaining balance is due within five business days after our final walkthrough.

Sincerely,
Colin Beck, Beck Builders

sections.title: Reading Part 3 · Reading for Information
sections.instructions: Read the article and answer the questions.
sections.passageTitle: The quiet return of the night train
sections.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, the overnight sleeper train was a fixture of European travel. Passengers boarded in the evening, slept through the miles, and woke in a different country. By the early 2000s, however, the service was in steep decline. Low-cost airlines had made short-haul flights cheaper and faster, and national rail operators, under pressure to cut costs, retired their sleeper routes one after another.

In the past decade, that trend has begun to reverse. Concerns about aviation emissions have led travellers to reconsider, and by some estimates a night train produces roughly eighty percent less carbon dioxide per passenger than a comparable short-haul flight. A Vienna-based operator that took over several abandoned routes in 2016 reports passenger numbers up by about thirty percent since 2019, and several countries have announced new overnight links.

Yet the revival faces stubborn obstacles. Manufacturers have not built sleeper carriages in decades, so operators rely on ageing rolling stock that is expensive to maintain and often unreliable. Track access fees, which vary widely between countries, can make cross-border journeys costly, and tickets on popular routes still run about twenty percent higher than budget airfares. Analysts also note that a night train must fill most of its berths to break even, which leaves little margin for error.

Supporters argue that comparing ticket prices alone overlooks what passengers actually receive. A sleeper journey replaces a night in a hotel, and it delivers travellers directly into city centres rather than distant airports. One operator has ordered thirty-three new trainsets with private compartments and en-suite showers, a move that suggests confidence in the market, although delivery is not expected for several years.

Whether the night train's comeback lasts may depend less on nostalgia than on policy. Governments that reduce track fees or subsidize equipment purchases could make the service competitive; those that do not may see the revival stall, leaving the night train an appealing but marginal option.

options: Governments should ban low-cost airlines

questions.explanation: The article describes the revival, the obstacles, and the role of policy.

options: New tracks made trains slower

questions.explanation: Low-cost airlines and cost-cutting rail operators led to retired routes.

questions.explanation: The article cites an estimate of about eighty percent less.

questions.explanation: It reports passenger numbers up about thirty percent since 2019.

questions.explanation: The article says it is expensive to maintain and often unreliable.

questions.label: Question 6
questions.question: What does "leaves little margin for error" imply?
options: The trains must be nearly full to make money
The trains must run exactly on schedule
Operators cannot afford any accidents
Ticket prices cannot be changed
questions.explanation: Because most berths must be filled to break even, there is little room for empty seats.

questions.label: Question 7
questions.question: What do supporters say about comparing ticket prices?
options: It proves trains are cheaper
It only matters for business travellers
It ignores that the train replaces a hotel night and arrives in city centres
It is unfair to airlines
questions.explanation: They argue sleepers replace a night in a hotel and reach city centres.

questions.label: Question 8
questions.question: What does the order for thirty-three trainsets suggest?
options: Some operators are confident about future demand, although the new trains are years away
Old carriages will be repaired immediately
Demand is already met
Track fees will be reduced next year
questions.explanation: The article says the order suggests confidence, but delivery is several years away.

questions.label: Question 9
questions.question: What does the author conclude about the future of night trains?
options: It is certain to succeed
It depends on airline ticket prices alone
It depends on nostalgia among passengers
It may depend on government policy on fees and subsidies
questions.explanation: The last paragraph ties the revival to policy such as track fees and equipment subsidies.

sections.title: Reading Part 4 · Reading for Viewpoints
sections.instructions: Read the two viewpoints and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
Pay Servers Fairly, Not Randomly
By Renata Silva

Tipping is a relic that asks customers to solve a problem employers should own. A server's income swings with the weather, the day of the week, and even a customer's mood, which makes budgeting for rent nearly impossible. Studies also suggest that tips are higher for servers who fit customers' expectations of appearance, meaning the system rewards bias more reliably than it rewards service. Countries without a tipping culture, such as Japan, still enjoy excellent service. If restaurants paid a living wage and built it into menu prices, servers would earn a stable income and diners would know what a meal truly costs.

Keep the Tip
By Daniel Cho

Abolishing tipping sounds fair, but it would hurt the people it claims to help. In a busy restaurant, a skilled server on a strong night can earn well above a typical hourly wage, and that upside attracts talented staff. If owners raise menu prices by eighteen to twenty percent to cover higher wages, many diners will simply eat out less, and slower business means fewer shifts for everyone. Tipping also gives customers a direct way to reward good service and to hold restaurants accountable. It is not perfect, but a system that rewards effort is better than one in which a mediocre server earns the same as an excellent one.

questions.label: Question 1
questions.question: What is the main topic of the two pieces?
options: Whether tipping in restaurants should be abolished
How restaurants set menu prices
How to improve service in Japan
Whether servers should receive training
questions.explanation: Both authors debate ending tipping.

questions.label: Question 2
questions.question: What is Silva's main criticism of tipping?
options: It makes menus more expensive
It lowers the quality of food
It shifts responsibility for wages from employers to customers
It is illegal in some countries
questions.explanation: She says tipping asks customers to solve a problem employers should own.

questions.label: Question 3
questions.question: How does Silva say tipping affects servers' incomes?
options: Their earnings are unpredictable, making budgeting difficult
Their earnings are always too low
Their earnings are guaranteed by law
Their earnings depend on years of experience
questions.explanation: She notes income swings with weather, weekday, and customer mood.

questions.label: Question 4
questions.question: What does Silva suggest about tips and appearance?
options: The system may reward bias more than service
Appearance has no effect on tips
Customers tip based on menu prices
Servers should dress formally
questions.explanation: She says tips favour servers who fit expectations of appearance.

questions.label: Question 5
questions.question: Why does Silva mention Japan?
options: To compare menu prices
To show that tipping originated there
To argue that servers are better paid abroad
To show that excellent service does not require tipping
questions.explanation: She says countries without tipping culture still enjoy excellent service.

questions.label: Question 6
questions.question: What outcome does Silva expect if restaurants pay a living wage?
options: Service would improve immediately
Restaurants would close
Menu prices would fall
Servers would have stable incomes and diners would know the true cost of a meal
questions.explanation: She says wages built into prices would produce stable income and clarity.

questions.label: Question 7
questions.question: What does Cho say about strong nights for skilled servers?
options: They lose money on slow days
They earn the same as any other night
They can earn well above a typical hourly wage
They receive bonuses from owners
questions.explanation: He says skilled servers can earn well above a typical wage on strong nights.

questions.label: Question 8
questions.question: What consequence of higher menu prices does Cho fear?
options: More customers tipping less
Owners earning higher profits
Servers demanding higher wages
Diners eating out less and servers getting fewer shifts
questions.explanation: He warns of less dining out and slower business, which means fewer shifts.

questions.label: Question 9
questions.question: What does Cho say tipping gives customers?
options: A guarantee of quality
A direct way to reward good service and hold restaurants accountable
A way to set menu prices
A discount on their meals
questions.explanation: He says tipping rewards service and holds restaurants accountable.

questions.label: Question 10
questions.question: On what point do the authors most directly disagree?
options: Whether tipping rewards effort or produces instability and bias
Whether servers deserve to be paid
Whether customers enjoy dining out
Whether restaurants should raise prices
questions.explanation: Silva says tipping rewards bias and creates instability; Cho says it rewards effort.

sections.title: Writing Task 1 · Email
sections.instructions: Write an email based on the task below.

writingTask.title: Writing an Email
writingTask.scenario: You lead a small design team. A supplier delay means you will deliver a project to an important client one week later than promised. Write an email to the client.
instructions: Explain what caused the delay and how long it will be.
Apologize and describe the effect on the client's plans.
Offer two options for moving forward.
writingTask.sampleAnswer: Dear Mr. Fraser, I am writing to inform you of a delay affecting the brand packaging project. Our printing supplier experienced a machine failure last week, and the finished materials will now reach us on June 21 instead of June 14. I sincerely apologize for the inconvenience, especially since I understand your product launch is scheduled for June 24. The revised date still leaves three days before the launch, but it removes the buffer we had planned for final review. To help, I can offer two options. First, we can courier the materials directly to your warehouse on the 21st, so you can review them on arrival and avoid an extra day of transit. Second, we can arrange a smaller first delivery of the most urgent items by June 17 and send the remainder on the 21st. Please let me know which option suits you best, and I will confirm the details the same day. Thank you for your patience and for your continued trust in our team. Kind regards, Amara Lewis

sections.title: Writing Task 2 · Survey Response
sections.instructions: Write a response to the survey questions below.

writingTask.title: Responding to Survey Questions
writingTask.scenario: Your city is deciding whether to turn a busy downtown street into a pedestrian-only zone, or keep it open to cars and widen the sidewalks. Complete the survey explaining which option you prefer and why.
instructions: Give at least two reasons for your choice, using specific examples.
Address one possible concern about your choice and respond to it.
writingTask.sampleAnswer: I prefer turning the street into a pedestrian-only zone. First, removing cars would make the area safer and quieter, which encourages people to linger. In cities that have done this, cafés and shops often report more customers because visitors walk slowly and notice storefronts. Second, the change would reduce air pollution in the busiest part of downtown, which benefits everyone who works or lives nearby. Some business owners worry that deliveries and customers who drive would be lost. This is a fair concern, but it can be addressed by allowing delivery vehicles in early morning hours and by placing clear signs to nearby parking garages. I also suggest running a six-month trial so the city can measure foot traffic and sales before making the change permanent. A trial would show whether the idea works for local businesses and give residents confidence in the decision. Thank you for allowing residents to have a say.

sections.title: Speaking Task 1 · Giving Advice
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 1: Giving Advice
speakingTask.scenario: A colleague was recently passed over for a promotion they worked hard for, and they are thinking about quitting. Give your colleague advice on how to handle this situation.
tips: Acknowledge the person's feelings first.
Give two or three practical, balanced suggestions.
Explain the reasoning behind your advice.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I understand how disappointing this must feel, especially after all your hard work. Before making a big decision, I would suggest taking a few days to cool down so you are not acting out of frustration. Then, ask your manager for specific feedback about what was missing and what you could do to be considered next time. That way you can decide if there is a real path forward. At the same time, it might be wise to quietly explore other opportunities, so you have options. Whatever you choose, remember that one setback does not define your career, and I'm here to support you.

sections.title: Speaking Task 2 · Talking about a Personal Experience
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 2: Talking about a Personal Experience
speakingTask.scenario: Describe a mistake you made that taught you an important lesson. Explain what happened and what you learned.
tips: Briefly describe the situation and the mistake.
Explain the consequences and how you responded.
End with the lesson and how you apply it now.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: A few years ago, I forgot to double-check a client's shipping address and sent an important package to the wrong city. The client was upset, and I felt terrible. I immediately called the courier, arranged an express redelivery at my own expense, and apologized directly. The package arrived one day late, and the client actually appreciated how quickly I responded. Since then, I always verify details before sending anything. That experience taught me that mistakes are manageable if you take responsibility quickly.

sections.title: Speaking Task 3 · Describing a Scene
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 3: Describing a Scene
speakingTask.scenario: Describe a community festival held at night beside a river. Include what you see, hear, and smell, and what people are doing.
tips: Use your senses to create a vivid picture.
Organize your description from a wide view to specific details.
Mention how the atmosphere feels.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: The riverbank glows with hundreds of paper lanterns, and their reflections shimmer on the dark water. Families crowd along the path, children waving glow sticks while a band plays cheerful folk music from a small stage. The air smells of roasted corn and fried dough from the food stalls, and vendors call out to passing crowds. Near the water, couples watch small lanterns float downstream. Everywhere there is laughter and a warm, relaxed feeling, as if the whole town has come together to celebrate.

sections.title: Speaking Task 4 · Making Predictions
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 4: Making Predictions
speakingTask.scenario: A man stands at a bus stop in the rain holding a large cake box. His phone is ringing, and a bus is approaching in the distance. Predict what will happen next and explain your reasoning.
tips: Base your predictions on details in the scene.
Use language of prediction such as will, probably, and might.
Include a beginning, a middle, and an ending.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I think the man is probably late for a birthday party, since he is carrying a cake. He will likely answer the phone quickly to tell the host he is on his way, while trying to keep the box dry under his arm. When the bus arrives, he will hurry aboard, and the box might get slightly squashed in the crowd. In the end, I believe he will arrive a little late but in good spirits, and everyone will laugh about the slightly damaged cake.

sections.title: Speaking Task 5 · Comparing and Persuading
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 5: Comparing and Persuading
speakingTask.scenario: Your manager is choosing a location for the annual team retreat. Option A is a two-day wilderness canoe trip costing $250 per person. Option B is a one-day workshop at a downtown hotel with a catered lunch, costing $120 per person. Persuade your manager to choose one option.
tips: State your choice at the start.
Compare cost, benefits, and practicality directly.
Anticipate one objection and respond to it.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I would recommend the downtown workshop. First, it costs only $120 per person, which is less than half the price of the canoe trip, and that saves money for other team needs. Second, a workshop offers structured activities that improve communication, while a canoe trip requires everyone to have the same fitness level and comfort with the outdoors. Some might say the canoe trip builds stronger bonds, but not everyone would enjoy it, and it takes two working days. A one-day workshop gives us focused teamwork with far less risk and disruption.

sections.title: Speaking Task 6 · Dealing with a Difficult Situation
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 6: Dealing with a Difficult Situation
speakingTask.scenario: A friend lent you her expensive camera for a weekend trip, and you accidentally dropped it and cracked the lens. Explain what you would say to your friend and what you would do to resolve the situation.
tips: Take responsibility without making excuses.
Explain what you would offer to do.
Show that you value the friendship.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I would tell her right away, in person if possible, so she doesn't hear it in a text. I would say, "I'm so sorry, I dropped your camera and cracked the lens, and I take full responsibility." I would offer to pay for the repair or replacement, and I would find out what it costs before we meet. I would also ask how she would prefer to handle it. Most importantly, I would make it clear that her trust matters more to me than the camera, and I would never borrow anything without extra care again.

sections.title: Speaking Task 7 · Expressing Opinions
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 7: Expressing Opinions
speakingTask.scenario: Some people believe employers should be required by law to let employees ignore work messages outside working hours. Do you agree or disagree? Support your opinion with reasons.
tips: State your opinion clearly at the start.
Give two or three reasons with examples.
Acknowledge a counterargument and respond.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: I agree that employees should have the right to disconnect. First, constant availability leads to burnout, because people never fully recover from work. Second, rest improves productivity, so employers benefit too when staff return refreshed. Third, without a clear rule, workers may feel pressured to reply at night, even if nobody asks them directly. Some argue that emergencies require flexibility, and that is a fair point. But the law could include exceptions for urgent situations and for jobs that need on-call duty. Overall, I believe healthy boundaries make workplaces fairer and more sustainable.

sections.title: Speaking Task 8 · Describing an Unusual Situation
sections.instructions: Prepare and speak using the prompt below.

speakingTask.title: Task 8: Describing an Unusual Situation
speakingTask.scenario: You see a photo of a library built inside an abandoned subway station, with bookshelves lining the platform and reading tables on the old tracks. Describe it to a friend and explain whether you think it is a good idea.
tips: Describe the most unusual features first.
Explain how visitors might experience it.
Give a clear opinion with reasons.
speakingTask.sampleAnswer: This library is remarkable. Bookshelves stretch along the old platform, and the reading tables sit where the trains used to run, so it feels like reading inside a piece of history. Visitors would probably find it quiet and atmospheric, though I imagine the lighting and temperature could be a challenge underground. Still, I think it is a wonderful idea, because it gives an unused space a new purpose and brings people into the community. I would definitely visit, and I would bring a sweater.
